doc.title: Larry Ridley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 10, 2003

title: Young leaders, the apprentice period and record industry contracts
summary: Young musicians used to apprentice with elders as Clifford Brown did; he criticizes the industry signing inexperienced youth.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: we just have to be a watchdog to make sure that people understand that we cannot have this sort of cookie cutter instantaneous way of producing things.

You know, people sometimes complain that some of the younger musicians are being elevated to the place of having their own bands and leadership and their own albums and they’re only in their early twenties or something. But then you go back and say well Clifford Brown was a leader at a young age.
But he was with Max Roach and was with Art Blakey.
Well that’s my question. What was the difference?

That’s one of the things that I wish would happen again. See because a lot of what I went through personally, like Clifford Brown and different ones, Horace Silver and all, any of the guys you want to name, Donald Byrd or Barry Harris. Any of us that were coming along, we played with the older musicians. It was an apprentice period that you served. Now there is so much industry involvement of record companies wanting to sign people. And then they sign a lot of young people because many of them, they don’t know what’s happening and they sign them to these really ridiculous contracts and there is so much — some of those contracts are some of the most ridiculous things you ever wanted to read in your life even if you don’t have a law degree. The record industry is something that is — it’s always been suspect, and rightfully so. Because there’s been a lot of chicanery and hook and crook stuff that has gone on. And artists and entertainers — not only in jazz but across the board and even in the acting business too — it’s the same thing. The arts and entertainment, the people who love it and are the people out there doing it are the ones that get misused. And I wish the apprentice period would come back some kind of way. Some of the college situations are serving like that too, and I’d like to see more of them developed along those lines whereas you get kids who come through — because the same question is going on in the NBA now. The kids coming right out of high school going into the NBA. But I think that there is something that’s lost if we don’t have — particularly in this music — because we’re talking about something that requires a long term commitment. Because some of these people, I mean they haven’t even developed. And it’s only rare that you’ll have this cream that rises to the top like a Clifford Brown or a Lee Morgan or you know like some of these talents that we’ve seen that come along in the past that suddenly really demonstrate something that you can’t quite define or describe. I don’t know how you describe it. You know because everybody’s trying to get to it and if we can find the formula we could bottle it and we could both make a million dollars. We could be partners, right? You know ‘cause that’s what we work with our students, trying to get them to understand. Because I constantly ask my students, well what do you want to do? They say I want to get a BMW, I want to have a house, I want to be a member of a country club. You know they talk about all the trappings that they want,
